en: The Scripture on the Samādhi of Pure Deliverance Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying on Mount Śakuntaka near Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
There were twenty-five thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats who had attained supernatural powers, were liberated from fear, and had transcended all terrors;
they were fearless regarding what is to be feared, unimpeded in the three liberations, and possessed the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Their minds were empty and tranquil, and they had all entered into the wisdom of emptiness; their eloquence was unimpeded. There were also seventy-eight thousand bodhisattvas.

They all abide in the Samādhi of Fearlessness and the Samādhi of Universal Radiance. Some have attained the Samādhi of Returning to Pure Precepts; some have already attained the Samādhi of Immovability;
some have already attained the Samādhi of Birth by Realization; and some have attained the Samādhi of the Rain of Dharma.

These Great Honored and Wise Ones possess skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and limitless wisdom-accumulation (*jñānasaṃbhāra*); their eloquence is peerless, and their perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is infinite. They have already...

Possessing the seven treasures of the Dharma, his mind is empty and unimpeded, pure as the moon reflected in water. Free from mind, intellect, and consciousness, he has already transcended the realm of death and crossed over to where there is no fear.
Fearing that which is itself fearless, his five eyes are clear and penetrating; he observes the three realms and the five paths, transforming and taking form through rebirth.
Enveloped by the net of perversions, their own sins and merits follow them, surrounding their bodies in an unceasing whirlpool.
Among the ranks of humans and beings with consciousness, those submerged in the ocean of craving suffer pain and distress without any awareness, yet they falsely claim it to be happiness.
Encountering hardship and calamity, they do not realize that their own deluded conduct brought it about, but instead resent Heaven; thus, their sorrow only increases.

Sorrow arises as the poison of a distracted mind; evil intentions flourish until, at the end of one's life, one enters the three miserable realms (*trāya*). There, one undergoes myriad forms of punishment and torture, equipped with all five poisons.

One suffers these transgressions for thousands of billions of kalpas. Although the retribution for physical offenses is exhausted, one transforms into an evil form and further receives the bodies of a hundred kinds of animals.
Emerging from one body to enter another, emerging from one consciousness to enter another, one forgets one's original consciousness and wanders on in this cycle.
The five realms of existence end and begin again; they revolve without limit, their currents flowing on without ceasing.

Beholding with one's own eyes the fear of birth and death within the three realms, one is drowned by the six desires. Like being submerged in the great ocean at Mount Sumeru, there is no time of escape.

Even though heaven and earth grow old and decay, and at the end of the kalpa are consumed by fire until the waters of the great ocean are utterly dried up, Mount Sumeru still has a time when it will emerge [from destruction].
Yet the multitudes of sentient beings within the triple world, submerged by the six desires, are in a state far more perilous than that of Mount Sumeru.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives this with clear discernment and takes pity on those who are ignorant, foolish, and wicked, who have not yet seen the disparities of birth and death, O World-Honored One.

He expounds the True Dharma, compassionately transforming the three realms and leading all across the five paths. He cuts off all pathways, extinguishes the fires of birth and death, and opens the gate of emptiness.
He brings beings peacefully into the abode of Nirvana, manifesting the discipline of mastery.

With the fetters of selflessness untied, he perceives the bonds of birth and death—the twelve roots of delusion and the sixty-two views—causing the multitude to be liberated from their fetters without obstruction. World-Honored One...
The Honored One transformed through his Way. His wholesome and beneficial deeds caused all devas, humans, and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to assist the World-Honored One.

He swept away the three realms and severed the three evil paths, opening the way to the three virtues. When the World-Honored One’s transformation was complete, he moved the hosts of Māra throughout the entire Buddha-field.
Heaven and earth shook six times; the colors of humans and devas changed, as did all the spirits and demons of Māra’s host.
The dragons, asuras, and their subordinates were all moved with agitation and unrest.

The various devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and asuras, each with their respective retinues, were all struck with fear in their own abodes and took refuge in the Buddha. The Buddha, moved by compassion for them all, emitted light from the white tuft between his eyebrows;
it went forth to bring peace to them, its radiance penetrating and illuminating the two heavens of the world and shining down upon the eighteen hells.
The realm of the Ultimate Buddha. Jiang Chang Zu-you was filled with joy; following the light, he arrived at the Buddha’s abode.

There were the various heavenly lords and Śakras, sons of heaven and princesses, the great honored ones of the heavens, the wondrous and sublime celestial deities, Māras, and their various officials and subordinates, the Lords of Records and the Lords of Fate, the Thirty-two Kings of the Settlements, the Pillar-of-Heaven Generals, and the Kings of Special Advancement. The Vinaya...

The Dharma-protectors known as Gongke Chechifulang, the Office of Merit (Gongcao) messengers, the Celestial Marquis Taichi, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, and the Crown Prince’s messengers all simultaneously followed the light to the Buddha’s abode.
They prostrated themselves, taking refuge at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him seven times.
Having completed their worship of the Buddha, they remained suspended in mid-air. So too did the various Dragon Kings and Asura Kings.
The subordinate officials followed the light and arrived; they prostrated themselves and took refuge, completing their worship of the Buddha. They then attended behind the Buddha.

The various heavenly kings—Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, up to the Heaven of the Thirty-two—and the various devaputras and auxiliary celestial generals, all held celestial flowers, incense, *ratnarāja* (jewel-kings), red pearls, *maṇi* jewels, *vaiḍūrya* (lapis lazuli), gold, and silver.
Crystal, *vaiḍūrya*, *musāragalva*, and *aśmagarbha* banners and silks; exquisite jewel canopies; famous incenses, blended incenses, and fragrant oils such as *tagara*;
and all manner of rare and precious treasures—all that exists in the heavens—were brought forth to offer to the World-Honored One and the various honored Bodhisattvas and great disciples.
All eighteen hells were completely stilled, and the prison officials and their subordinates all followed the light.
They arrived. They took refuge and prostrated themselves. They circumambulated the Buddha one hundred and twenty times, striking their heads in repentance for their transgressions.
Having completed their worship, they stood to the right of the Buddha. These were the corrupt officials of hell:
King Xuandu, King Shengdu, King Guangwu, King Jinping, King Xuanyang, King Wuyang, King Gongyang, King Pingyang, King Guangjin, King Dutang, and King Yuanwei.

The King of Hu-pei, the King of Lian-shi, the Superintendent of Water Officials, the Superintendent of Iron Officials, the Superintendent of Fire Officials, the Superintendent of Artisans, and the Superintendent of Civil Officials—these eighteen messengers, each leading their respective subordinate officials, followed the light and arrived.

They prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, took the triple refuge three times, repented of their transgressions, and offered their thanks. They circumambulated the Buddha seventy times and bowed in reverence.
The King Bimbisāra arrived at the place where the Buddha was with a retinue of one billion followers.

Two million five hundred thousand laymen and laywomen also came and sat together in the assembly; in total, several million people gathered and sat down, occupying the left side to listen to the Buddha preach the sutras.
At that time, the people of the kingdom were afflicted by a pestilence, and the ministers and subjects were acting wickedly and facing great peril. The Buddha—
He felt compassion for them, fearing they would fall into the three miserable realms and be submerged in bitter suffering.

Desiring to deliver and liberate them, he returned to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and manifested transformations that moved all hearts; there was none who did not receive deliverance. The Buddha then addressed the fourfold assembly, as well as the devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits.
"Āsuras, yakṣas, gandharvas, mahoragas, ghosts and spirits, and the officials and subordinates of Yama, all listen attentively.
Each says, 'Yes, yes; we shall obey. We now receive the Buddha’s teaching; we pray that you will grant us your holy transformation and deign to bestow upon us your compassionate instruction."
"You should practice this accordingly. The Buddha said: "Sentient beings of the three realms who consume blessings without practicing conduct fall back into hell.
Those who harbor malice toward living beings die and enter hell. Those who engage in flattery, deception, and fraud die and enter hell.

Those who greedily seek profit without ceasing, whose hearts harbor envy and jealousy, who are arrogant and self-willed, and who watch one another for opportunities to mutually harm and injure, die and enter hell. [Those who are] upright and just..."
They harbor mutual jealousy; they are treacherous and sycophantic, harboring enmity toward one another. Those who are heterodox yet always consider themselves upright die and enter hell.

Those who kill, steal, commit adultery, practice deception, speak falsehoods, engage in double-tongued speech, use harsh words, revile others, or utter curses die and enter hell. Those who drink wine and become intoxicated, who covet beauty and indulge in lustful desires [likewise fall].
If one harms living beings for the sake of a tasty meal, upon death they enter hell. If one is stingy and greedy, eating alone, upon death they enter the realm of hungry ghosts.

If one harbors much anger and displays joy or wrath at improper times, upon death they become a lowly person. If one owes debts but does not repay them, or borrows money but does not return it, and holds their head high while excessively provoking others, they will later become an animal.
If one discusses flattery, they will later become a ghost or spirit. If one lacks any sense of reliance or moral support, plants blessings yet remains full of rage, [the results] will be combined.

Those who harbor poisonous hatred will later become dragons or snakes. Those whose precepts are weak yet who pride themselves on their status, and who delight in being lords of men, will, if their five perfections are impure, fall into hell after death.
Those whose five precepts are complete and firm will become humans after death. If their practice of the ten wholesome deeds is weak, they will be born in the heavens below the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

If their ten wholesome deeds are firm yet they still possess desire, they will be born in the heavens below the six heavens of the desire realm. Through the first dhyāna, one is born in the form realm; through the second dhyāna...
They are born in the formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*). Those who do not understand emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in the third dhyāna are born in the twenty-four heavens above;

yet they do not escape the suffering of hell. All categories of sentient beings and their various forms arise each from their own mind, obtained through the seeds of their past actions (*karmavipāka*).
When gods and humans perform divine conduct, they obtain a celestial body; when they perform human conduct, they obtain a human body; and the same applies to nāgas, ghosts, and spirits.
During one's lifetime, if one accumulates poison and anger, delights in wearing head-wraps and leaning against trees, this constitutes the conduct of a dragon; upon death, one becomes a dragon.
If one practices the conduct of a ghost or spirit, one falls among ghosts and spirits. If one practices the conduct of an animal, one falls among animals.
By practicing the conduct of a slave, one falls among slaves; by practicing the conduct of a hungry ghost, one falls among hungry ghosts; by practicing the conduct of hell, one falls into hell.
Through patience, one obtains a handsome appearance that others delight to behold; through anger, one obtains ugliness. Through respect, one obtains longevity and honor;
through arrogance, one obtains short stature and lowliness. By planting suffering, one reaps suffering; by planting happiness, one reaps happiness. Thus it is done.

This is obtained through this; if one does not perform this, then this is not obtained. You all have each cultivated your own respective practices, and according to those practices you receive retribution.

Thus, there now exist various kinds of beings whose received forms differ: why is it that they are unequal in terms of noble or base, high or low status, beauty or ugliness, and tallness or shortness?
It arises from the mind. Because mental thoughts differ, such retributions result. This applies to all devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits.
The Kings of Hell, the four classes of people, and the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas heard the Buddha’s exposition of the true and correct Great Dharma concerning the verification of sins and blessings.
It was indeed as the World-Honored One had taught through his compassionate transformation: that forms and types differ, and the various deities are immeasurable;
yet each, according to their own original nature and state of mind, declared that they would receive the teaching and practice it, fundamentally eliminating ignorance from this point forward.
First, establishing conduct is the foundation.

The Buddha said: "One who can practice the four debts of gratitude and the four immeasurables, enter the concentration of emptiness through the absence of conceptualization and the absence of aspiration, establish the eight righteous practices, the eight applications of effort, and the nine successive concentrations, and eliminate the nine modes of thought—such a person, by means of the ten dharmas of concentration, shall depart from birth and death and attain [liberation]."
They transcend the three realms and do not fear the hardships of the three miserable paths. They tread upon blades without being wounded and walk through fire without being burned;
they dwell amidst desire without defilement and remain unharmed even in the midst of calamity. Thus they attain equal enlightenment.

Śāriputra, rising from his seat, adjusting his robes, and joining his palms while kneeling with bended knee, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "The devas, humans, ghosts, spirits, nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, and..."
“Kumbhāṇḍas, Piśācas, Mahoragas, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, birds, and beasts—their consciousnesses are of one kind, yet their realms differ and their inclinations are not uniform.
How is it that they receive retribution according to their sins and merits? The Buddha said:

“Sentient beings receive physical forms in accordance with their conduct and obtain their karmic fruits. As for the places where they fall, each follows what they have practiced, thereby bringing about either calamity or fortune.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "All dharmas are fundamentally pure. For what reason are there offenses and blessings?

Dharmas are fundamentally non-dual, and the mind is fundamentally and originally non-existent. How could there be a threefold division? Even two thousand [dharmas] are fundamentally non-existent, such that not even one exists; how much more so two?"
The mind has no fundamental basis. The mind has no male or female. The mind has no large or small. The mind has no noble or base. The mind has no diversity.
The mind is empty and void, like the emptiness of nirvāṇa. The mind is as empty as original non-existence. The formlessness of the mind makes it the abode of the spirit.

The spirit is likewise formless. When the spirit departs, the spirit is empty; when phenomena are empty, they are like the emptiness of the spirit. The emptiness of the spirit is as if originally non-existent.

The three realms are empty, the five paths are empty, the myriad things are empty, and the four great elements are empty—earth, water, fire, and wind are all empty, being equal and without distinction.
The self is empty; the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, mind, consciousness—these eight are fundamentally empty. They have been empty from the beginning and are fundamentally pure.
Form is fundamentally empty and pure. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are fundamentally empty and pure. The self is fundamentally pure. Body and mind are fundamentally pure.
The three realms are fundamentally pure. Sentient beings and things are fundamentally pure. The six bases—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—are fundamentally pure.
Earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are fundamentally pure. Blue, red, white, and black are fundamentally...
Pure. Characters and words are also empty and fundamentally pure. All dharmas are empty and pure. The *prajñāpāramitā* is fundamentally pure.
The three realms are like an illusion; persons are also like an illusion. Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like an illusion.
The five aggregates and the six sense bases are also like an illusion. The birth of form and the death of form, the arising of form and the ceasing of form, are impermanent and like an illusion.

Illusion. Sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—consciousness arises and consciousness ceases; they are impermanent and like an illusion. Birth, old age, sickness, and death are impermanent and like an illusion.
Hunger, thirst, cold, and heat are impermanent and like an illusion. The four great elements are not real; form perishes and quickly decays.
All things return to impermanence. Consider that originally there was no form; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness were also originally non-existent.

The self was originally non-existent; the five aggregates and the six sense-fields were originally non-existent. Earth, water, fire, wind, and clouds were originally non-existent; all dharmas were originally non-existent.

The three realms are fundamentally non-existent. Sentient beings and persons are fundamentally non-existent. The existence of a self, a world, a self-possessed world, "mine," and "not-mine" are fundamentally non-existent.
The states of perception and non-perception are fundamentally non-existent. Even the notion of a Buddha abiding as such is fundamentally non-existent.

Because the Buddha has compassion for the world, he manifests a Buddha-body to lead sentient beings back, causing them to return to the fundamental non-existence of the spirit. This fundamental non-existence is without dwelling; it neither comes nor goes.
There is nothing to be relinquished and nothing to be grasped; no attachment and no bondage; no birth and no death; neither existing nor ceasing. It is as tranquil as empty space;

neither arising nor perishing; without increase and without decrease; without suffering and without pleasure; without sorrow and without the absence of sorrow. The nature of the mind is fundamentally non-existent.
This is the returning of the spirit. Returning means going back to original non-being (*mūla-asvabhāva*). It is like a person who has traveled far away as a guest;
having lived in another land for many years in poverty and distress, he repeatedly commits offenses while abroad and is imprisoned.

The jailers are cruel and malicious, subjecting him to harsh and poisonous torture, employing all five kinds of agonizing punishments. His spirit is despondent; alone and solitary, he dwells as a sojourner in a foreign land, his body confined within the prison.

Within, he saw the gates; preserving his body, he had no means to purchase its release. Without, he had no acquaintances—no father, elder brother, wife, or children—and he was far from his native village.
Since there was no one who knew him, he suffered the utmost misery and calamity; starving, he could not obtain food, and though exhausted, he managed to escape. Now he has returned home once more.
Their bodies shall attain peace and security; they shall not lack food or clothing, and their happiness shall be boundless.

When people emerge from the terrors of birth and death, aging, illness, and death, and from the suffering of the hells, and instead find their way back to the fundamental non-arising, resting their spirits in nirvana—would this not be cause for joy?
The Buddha said: “It is so, it is so. Sentient beings obtain happiness from suffering; they obtain healing from pain; they obtain [nourishment] from hunger.”
When hungry, they receive nourishment; when cold, they receive warmth; when dying, they receive life; when poor, they receive wealth.
That person undergoes these various sufferings many times over before finally escaping them all. Once every matter is joyful, how could that person not rejoice?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "That person’s former suffering has now become joy; their immense delight is beyond words.
The Buddha said, "When a person emerges from the great cycle of birth and death and attains the crossing over to nirvāṇa, the unconditioned, their happiness is infinite.

What they wished for has already been attained; their mind follows its own resolve. Their task is finished; they are free from all feverish afflictions and will no longer undergo birth and death. Their spirit remains."

[He attained] mastery and long achieved liberation. At that time, among the great assembly seated there—consisting of devas and humans—who heard Mañjuśrī explain the special nature of original non-arising (*an-utpāda*), one thousand bhikṣus understood the meaning and, with their outflows exhausted, all attained arhatship (*arhat*).

Eight thousand bodhisattvas all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Eighty thousand devas and humans all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas. Five...
One thousand devas conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment; eight hundred laymen of pure faith all attained the patience of joy;
five hundred bhikṣus conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment; and sixty bhikṣuṇīs, their outflows exhausted, attained liberation of mind.
One million devas and humans attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena. Two hundred laywomen (*upāsikā*) all attained the stage of the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).

When this Dharma was being preached, the eightfold voice of the Great Being reached upward to the Brahma-heaven and downward was heard throughout the three miserable realms; the sufferings of those in hell and the hungry ghosts were stilled.
Hearing the sound of the Jewel of the Dharma, they all resolved to attain supreme, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Even the beasts and winged birds [did the same].
While hunting, they heard the sound of the Dharma and gave rise to wholesome thoughts. Vowing that upon the completion of this present life they might attain the human path, they resolved:
"We shall become śramaṇas and practice the Buddha-way. The kings, wardens, and officials of the hells all likewise gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment.

The devas, nāgas, and spirits all gave rise to hearts of compassion. Among the people of the land, those who were ill immediately took refuge [in the Buddha] and likewise resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "The various classes of devas, humans, and all sentient beings have all undergone the sufferings of the three miserable realms.
Now, they have all given rise to a mind of compassion; by virtue of this wholesome mind, they may all attain deliverance. The Buddha told him, "This applies to all categories of devas and humans."
When the mind, intellect, and consciousness are purified, one may then attain complete liberation. The Buddha immediately emitted light from his physical form;

its five colors were brilliant and dazzling, pervading as many Buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges River. Those who beheld this light attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena and, following the light, realized the six dharmas, fully entering into the practice of the Vinaya.
Even those in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, wild beasts, and winged creatures followed the light and resolved their minds upon the aspiration for enlightenment.
Bixing received the precepts and became a śramaṇa; he practiced pure transformation and sought the Buddha-way. All the devas and people attained the pure precepts.
Twenty-two thousand ordinary people all attained the Way and likewise sought the five precepts to become laymen and laywomen of pure faith (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*).
The Buddha then granted them the five precepts. Yama, King of the Hells, rose, adjusted his robes, and composed his heart and mind.
He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I am in charge of one hundred and thirty-four hells. Among them is the Great Niraya (Great Hell), where there are several thousand billions of millions of male and female offenders, beyond all counting.
Within the Great Niraya are eight medium Nirayas; within each medium Niraya are thirty small Nirayas; and within each small Niraya..."
The hells consist of ninety-six minor hells, measuring one thousand li, two thousand li, four thousand li, eight thousand li, sixteen thousand li, and even several tens of thousands of li.
They are filled with sinners, and there are also supervising officials and minor kings within them.
"May all governors, prefects, commandants, the five officials, and messengers be entirely subject to me. O World-Honored One, God among Gods, grant a great amnesty;
may the great trichiliocosm receive deliverance. Since my life has not yet ended, whom shall I govern? The Buddha told King Nimi:
"Grant a full pardon for all one hundred and thirty-four prisons. Furthermore, extend this to all hungry ghosts, spirits, gods, nāgas, asuras, birds, and wild beasts."
Release them. In this way, before long, the king’s prisons will be filled; it will not take more than a single day. O King, do not be distressed.
You ought to give rise to a heart of compassion and pity for sentient beings. You must not seek fame by contending with celestial kings, Māras, and asuras for the sake of reputation.
One cannot be honored merely because one rules over many subjects. If you wish to seek honor and nobility for kalpas on end, you must observe the five precepts.
Observe the precepts. Practice the six perfections, the four debts of gratitude, the four immeasurables, the four dhyānas, and the four noble truths.

Exercise patience and gentleness, practice giving, and harmonize the mind with broad benevolence. Have compassion for all sentient beings and rescue those in distress. Lower yourself before the world;

diminish and abandon all strength, excellence, and prideful thoughts. Eradicate greed and lust, severing the seeds of the demon of desire. Establish conduct of purity. O King, you should contemplate this.
Examine the people of the realm to see for what crimes they are punished under the filial governance. Among the people of the realm, it is not the virtuous who are punished;

rather, only those who are rebellious, immoral, unrighteous, lacking in benevolence, compassion, propriety, and faithfulness—those who are stingy and greedy, who do not believe in the Triple Gem, and who lack gratitude—are punished.
It is only the covetous, lustful, envious, and ignorant who are dealt with, regardless of whether they are noble or lowly.
Lowly beings, their offenses are unified under one principle. It makes no distinction between male or female, young or old, beautiful or ugly;

among all sentient beings, those who commit evil receive retribution for their evil, and those who cultivate merit receive reward for their merit. They are recorded by their own deeds of evil and merit, such that there is no place on earth—whether sea, mountain, or rock—that can hear them out.
"Desist! Do not undergo death. The King said, "I shall surely obey your instruction. He immediately took it to heart and upheld it, never failing the noble teaching.
He constantly proclaimed the True Dharma to transform and guide the offenders, causing them to give rise to wholesome minds and attain liberation from their sorrow and suffering.
The Bodhisattva Dharmeśvara addressed the Buddha, saying: "How can the sentient beings of the three realms attain mastery?

Those who wish to reach the unsurpassed, right, and true Great Way and thereby achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, who seek to sever the burning afflictions of birth and death within the three miserable realms, who desire to eliminate their own calamities and uproot the charges of hell, and who would prune away the five [hindrances]..."

The Red Registers of the Officials record those who cross over the hardships of coming and going within the three realms. They uproot the source of birth and death and eliminate the names from the registers of the five destinies.
They restore the spirit to its original non-being, sweep away the defilements of conceptualization within the three realms, purify the dwellings of the six spirits, and level the path to Nirvāṇa.
For the sake of sentient beings, they open the gate of Nirvāṇa and block the rivers of the three flows, severing [the cycle of rebirth].
Regarding the path of birth and death, how are its difficulties and ease? The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmeśvara: "You possess great compassion and pity;

you are able to shoulder the heavy responsibility for all sentient beings and take concern for the various classes of people throughout the world. It is precisely because you wish to deliver them that you have asked this question.
The Buddha then told the Bodhisattva Dharmeśvara and the Great Beings among sentient beings: "Listen all with clear attention."
Reflect upon this well and internalize it within your heart. The Buddha said: "Fools delight in birth and death, like those dwelling amidst the *ju-chi* (marshes).

Indulging their passions and letting their minds run wild, they plant the roots of birth and death for themselves. They revolve through the five realms, thereby establishing registers for the five stations."
Bound and fettered within the five realms of existence, they wander on without rest; all this is sown by the mind. Greed is the path to death;
ignorance is the mire in which one sinks and cannot emerge. Envy is the root of transgression; craving for profit leads to one's own ruin.

One who does not cease from lust in old age, who does not study in the night, and who possesses wealth yet neither gives in charity nor receives [the Dharma], is as the Buddha said: "One who possesses these eight qualities is..."
One deceives oneself; through heedlessness, one enters the three miserable realms. A hundred offenses arise from the mind; the mind is the sovereign of nirvana. The Way resides within one's own body;
it is brought forth by one’s own mind and is not sought from others. How could there be anything difficult about that which is obtained from others?
This is indeed difficult: the mind’s entry and exit have no gate through which it comes and goes; it circulates and wanders aimlessly, with no place where it dwells or stops.
The mind has no beginning or end, nor does it have a starting point. It is without form or image, neither distant nor near, neither "that" nor "this."
There is neither great nor small; neither old nor young; neither beautiful nor ugly; neither male nor female. The nature of the mind is such;
birth and death are natural; sin and merit are natural; the Way and its teachings are natural. The high-minded practitioner controls and stills the mind so that the Dharma is natural.
This is Nirvana, the orderly sequence of the Noble Truths. One enters the Eightfold Right Path, rejects the eight wrong occupations, eliminates the nine thoughts, and seeks the ten [virtues].

Through wisdom, one attains the ten powers and is entirely free from fear. By accumulating merit through the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), one reaches *nirvāṇa*—tranquil, unconditioned, unmoving, and unshakable;

neither arising nor non-arising, neither dying nor non-dying. Solely extricating oneself and emerging, one extinguishes the suffering of the three realms and removes the registers of the five destinies.
Walking alone without fear, one attains peerless conduct and enters the gate of the Great Dharani. One attains...
By means of the Samādhi of Boundless Depth, one then attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Bodhisattva Dharmeśvara addressed the Buddha, saying: "The mind attains mastery;

for what reason are there so many varieties [of states], such that one is recorded in the registers by the lords of the five destinies, and the name of birth and death is not eliminated? The Buddha said: "As for the mind, the mind does not see the mind."

There are those who possess a mind yet do not know that the mind is spontaneous. They revere their own minds and allow their minds to lead them. When they contemplate good within their hearts, they immediately speak and act accordingly;

when they contemplate evil within their hearts, they immediately speak and act accordingly. Their minds lack discernment; their minds are deluded in conduct; their minds are ignorant and their intentions are foolish.
One calculates that the body is permanent and cherishes it, claiming it as one's own; one first desires to provide it with bathing, combing, fine clothing, and delicious food.
One runs hither and thither, undergoing toil and exerting effort in thought, seeking wealth, treasures, official rank, and emoluments.

With perfumes, flowers, and necklaces, they adorn this body seeking honor; yet names are certainly empty, and emptiness possesses nothing. The three realms are not their children, for they seek empty fame.

Deceived by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), volition (*saṃskāra*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and the six decays—they sow the seeds of birth and death.
Thus they revolve through arising and passing away, coming and going without end.

The "bonds" refer to the five paths of existence. All seek after desire and affection, which constitute the root of birth and death. These phenomena are impermanent, and human beings likewise do not abide;
they flow constantly like water, resembling illusions and transformations. Birth and death occur suddenly, and there is neither constant form nor constant name.
For those who let their minds run wild in the pursuit of desires, their cravings increase all the more. They greedily pursue forms day and night, yet they remain long separated from true love.

Thus, one has no affliction with greed. The mind of desire serves as the field; insatiable conduct serves as the seed. By severing greed and eliminating the karma of profit, one departs from craving and is free from sorrow and affliction.
From this, one uproots the source of suffering and casts off suffering to ascend to the Purple Hall.

Forever freed from the distress of birth and death, one ultimately exists no more. Attaining mastery over the five locations, one completely extinguishes the divine register and no longer employs the regulation of life.
He is honored and revered by all people, like a sovereign emperor; none can surpass him alone. For this reason, they prostrate themselves in worship.

When the Buddha spoke these words, ten thousand bodhisattvas in the assembly all attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression); eight hundred bhikṣus all attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena);
seventy thousand devas and humans all attained the *dharma-rati-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of delighting in the Dharma); and three hundred thousand devas and humans...
They resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path. Three hundred thousand laymen of pure faith all attained the *kṣānti* of compliance with the Dharma.
One hundred thousand laywomen of pure faith all attained the *kṣānti* of joy. Five thousand bhikṣuṇīs all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.
Six hundred thousand spirits, ghosts, and dragon kings all returned to the gate of *dhāraṇī*. [The deities] Si-li and Si-ming... thirty.
The two regional ministers, King Jinwang, General Fuzhen, the Crown Prince, and the messengers all attained the Samādhi of Pure Radiance;
their entire retinue attained the stage of Non-returner (Anāgāmin). The Great King of the Five Realms and his attendants fully attained the stage of the Wanderer (Sakṛdāgāmin).
There were one hundred and thirty-seven minor kings of the hells, all of whom attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
Among the officials and subordinates, there were one billion who attained the patience of faith (*kṣānti*). A total of one billion men and women all attained the fruit of the path (*śrotāpanna*);
none failed to cross over. Their illnesses were cured; the blind regained their sight, the deaf regained their hearing, and those with ailments...
Those who were able to speak, such as the *kubjaka* (hunchbacked), regained their hands and feet. Women who were pregnant found safety for both mother and child.
Birds and wild beasts that heard the Dharma all, at the end of their lives, were reborn in the heavens.

The various heavenly lords and Śakra all held seven-jeweled lotuses, along with famous incense, *ke-fragrance*, unguents, blended perfumes, silk banners, flower canopies, celestial flags, and streamers. Thus they [honored it].

They made offerings. The devas, sons of gods, and jade maidens each held flowers, incense, banners, silks, and various rare jewels, scattering them all over the Buddha, as well as upon the bodhisattvas and the great bhikṣus.
Through the majestic transformation of the World-Honored One, a great palace was manifested, at which all were filled with joy.
They uttered the sounds of the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and all prostrated themselves at the feet of the Buddha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, together with three hundred ministers and elders, rose from their seats, joined their palms, knelt with bended knees, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"While we were within the great cycle of birth and death, submerged in the foul sea, we experienced the five poisons, suffering and pleasure, and all the various realms.
We were governed by the terrors of old age, sickness, and death; our grief and suffering were beyond words. The Buddha said: "All sentient beings..."
Regarding those within the great cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), there are ten types of habitual suffering. What are these ten? First, the suffering of birth;
second, the suffering of old age; third, the suffering of illness; fourth, the suffering of separation from what is loved; fifth, the suffering of all that is disagreeable;
sixth, the suffering of enmity and the suffering of dwelling among those one hates; seventh, the suffering of grief and anxiety; eighth, hunger and thirst.
Suffering. Ninth is the suffering of cold and poverty; tenth is the suffering of death. Furthermore, there are three sufferings:

first, the suffering of hell; second, the suffering of hungry ghosts; third, the suffering of animals. Furthermore, there are two sufferings: first, the suffering of spirits, ghosts, and nāgas; second, the suffering of lacking self-mastery.
All these are sufferings resulting from habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). When all habitual tendencies are exhausted, suffering ceases. This is...
The ten habitual practices belong to the Five Officials; the Five Officials belong to Yama; Yama belongs to the Buddha.
King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have a younger brother who has violated the precepts. I do not know to which government office he belongs, nor what offense he has committed.
He has been ill for three years and has not yet recovered. A World-Honored One is difficult to encounter; I pray that you will explain his situation. If you would..."
If the transgression is great, one shall die immediately upon falling ill; if the transgression is small, one should not suffer from a prolonged illness.
Heaven and Earth hear everything. How many palaces, government offices, and supervisory bureaus are there? How many classes of people commit how many offenses to constitute transgressions?
What constitutes a small offense, and what offense constitutes a great transgression? The deaths of humans differ: some die in old age, while others die in their prime.
There are those who die young; those who die of illness; those who die naturally; those killed by government officials; those killed by bandits;

those who die by fire; those who die by water; those who die of hunger; those who die of cold; those who die of thirst; and those killed by oxen or horses—such are the various modes of death. Where do their spirits and souls go?
We pray that the Buddha will deign to show compassion, reveal the truth to us who are blind and ignorant, and cause us to understand.
[The King] asked, "Do you know the prohibitions and defenses?
Is there anything that can be avoided? The Buddha told the King: "If an ordinary person has neither precepts nor practices the seven matters, at death they shall belong to hell.

They will be recorded by the five officials who oversee their life-span, and shall be subject to the Son of Heaven of Hell. This Son of Heaven is named Yama; he presides over the realm of the Buddha. All...
The heavenly beings, humans, ghosts, spirits, dragons, birds, and beasts—all are entirely subject to the Son of Heaven. There are eight minor kings;
furthermore, there are thirty states under the *Furong* kings. Each of these *Furong* kings, in turn, governs ninety-six subordinate states.

Each has its own distinct jurisdiction. Furthermore, there are the Outer Supervisors, the Five Officials, the General Commandant for Surveillance, the Registrar, the Eight Kings, the Office of the Imperial Scribe, and others.

Together with the Great General of the Hidden Night and the Officers of the Household Cavalry, they receive the celestial tally of the Heavenly Emperor and, along with the Great Kings of the Five Paths, on the days of the Eight Kings, move as swiftly as the wind to conduct secret inspections and tour the heavens, the people, and the various realms. They [examine] the...
The Di tribes hunt various species of birds to discern good from evil. There are many varieties, numbering in the hundreds of millions across tens of thousands of li.

They are distributed throughout the borders of Jiang, where their respective officials conduct investigations. The sovereign, ministers, and subjects record virtues and document faults, submitting these reports to the Emperor for his consideration.
The King of Fuyong reported this in turn to the eight kings; the eight kings, in turn, reported it to the Great King; and the Great King reported it to the Son of Heaven.

Regarding the offenses committed by the people, there were twenty matters in total. The most serious was said to be the loss of one's person; having died, one would no longer have a master and would consequently fall into the three miserable realms.
Forever without turning back, for incalculable billions of koṭis of kalpas, they emerge as beasts and predators.
Twenty evil deeds lead people into thirty-eight places of great suffering within the Great Mire (Mahāpaṅka). Within this mire, there are individual cities and walls.
There are eight great kings and thirty minor kings. The first is King Pinghu, who presides over the Mahāniraya (Great Hell of Unrelenting Torment).
Within it is a vast cauldron, forty *li* in length and breadth, and its depth is likewise;

it is filled with offenders solely for their killing of living beings, sexual misconduct, theft, lack of filial piety, and failure to observe propriety. The second is King Jinping, who governs the Kālasūtra (Black Rope) Hell.
Within it are iron ropes, and blades with three edges—some four-pronged, some eight-pronged—which tear the human body apart.

There are the precepts of the saw that dissects the person and the axe that hacks the human body, whether into four sides or eight corners. This is solely for sitting upon the commission of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and killing living beings;

for using soft-headed mallets, knives, and axes to harm humans and animals; and for lust, theft, jealousy, anger, and delusion. The third is King Maṅdu, who presides over the administration and punishment [of these offenses].
The Iron Prison (Ayas-tāla) torments the bodies of those who, while merely sitting, have crushed people or various sentient beings under their feet; it is like crushing sesame stalks in oil.

The fourth Heavenly King, Vaiśravaṇa, presides over the Hell of Conjunction (Saṃghāta). Within it are great iron nails that pierce the hundred joints of a person's body, causing pain that penetrates throughout the entire frame.
From the sky, great stones naturally rain down, shattering the person's body until it is as small as...
Noodles. Yet, while sitting [in meditation], they slander the Holy Path; they harbor poisonous thoughts toward the Buddhas, the True Persons, and the Bodhisattvas;

they commit rebellion and filial impiety; they sever the Dharma and sever merit; they treat their parents, teachers, friends, and those worthy of respect with contempt; and they slaughter living beings without the Way.

It is because of these calamities that the Fifth Holy Lord King presides over the prisons of Mount Tai. As soon as a person enters the mountain, the mountain spontaneously closes, shattering [all hope of escape].
The bones and flesh of the person's body are crushed; excrement and urine are mixed with the fragments like the juice of *tṛphala* grapes.

This is solely due to the commission of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), as well as jealousy, folly, hatred, self-exaltation, contempt for others, disobedience toward parents, teachers, friends, sovereigns, and the righteous teachings of one’s peers, and the resulting acts of factionalism, theft, lewdness, deception, and killing.
The sixth is the King of the Mysterious Metropolis (*Emendū Wang*), who presides over the Great City Prison.

Fire burns people; their bodies are scorched and consumed until nothing remains. This is solely because they deceived others and lacked faith, living off the food and clothing of others while being greedy for profit and refusing to practice generosity.
They enslaved and stripped others bare, which resulted from their own greed for fine garments. This was the seventh king, King Guangwu.

It primarily governs the Sword-Tree Hell. Within this hell, a gale of wind blows, driving a chaotic rain of swords and blades that hack and rend the bodies of those within until not a patch of skin remains intact.
Furthermore, they are devoured by great vultures. This is solely because they engaged in butchery, slaughter, hunting, and trapping, harboring evil intentions in every thought;

thus, they undergo this retribution. The eighth is King Wuyang, who presides over the Howling Hell. Within it, there are dogs that sever people's heads, drinking their blood and devouring their flesh. This is solely because...

Those who, while sitting, mentally, verbally, or physically commit acts of killing humans or animals; those who hire others to kill people; and those who instruct others to take life—due to these causes, they incur this calamity.
The ninth is the Lord of the Yang-Wang Prison, which governs the eighth path of hell. Within it, there are sharp swords that cover the ground with no space between them.

When a person walks upon them, their feet and ankles are sliced and severed. This occurs simply because one took pleasure in committing acts of violence and lacked a heart of compassion throughout one's entire life.
They destroy the bridge of the Dharma and harm sentient beings; by forcibly teaching others to transgress prohibitions, they bring about this calamity.

The tenth is King Dūyāṅga, who presides over the Prison of Thorny Trees. In this prison, the thorns on the trees are three *zhang* long. As soon as a person climbs the tree, the thorns point downward and pierce them;
as soon as they descend, the thorns point upward and pierce through them. The bodies of those people are all mangled and wounded, solely because they lacked the precepts.
Receiving the offerings of the faithful, wearing precious garments and ornaments, yet constantly pierced by spears and swords;
armored and girt with helmets, he cherished his own body while despising others, envying and harming sentient beings, thereby incurring this ultimate calamity. The eleventh is King Xiaoyang.
This primarily governs the Hell of Boiling Ashes. Within this hell is a river of hot, boiling ash. Upon entering it, one's entire body is completely scorched and dissolved.

This is solely because, in life, one ate sheep and roosters for their palatable taste, drank wine to the point of confusion, and lay upon śramaṇas as if using them for a pillow, uttering evil words from the mouth and lacking any heart of compassion;
thus one incurs this calamity. The twelfth is King Yanwei, who presides over the Great [Hell].

They enter the hell of devouring, where iron walls enclose them. Its gates are opened and great fires break out on all sides, burning those sinners solely because they slandered the Triple Gem and virtuous people, set mountains and marshes ablaze, harmed the lives of sentient beings, and stripped others of their clothing.

Those who slander and harm others, who are unfilial toward the Three Honored Ones and their two parents, and who are arrogant, self-indulgent, and lack precepts and faith, bring upon themselves these ultimate calamities.
The thirteenth [hell], King Vistara (Broad Progress), presides over the Great Avīci Hell. There, they are punished with the five poisons.
Their human bodies are dismembered and stretched out like a hide being tanned; they are pinned down with great nails driven into their hearts, hands, feet, and joints.

It pervades all. Furthermore, the eyes, tongue, ears, and nose are all permeated. It is solely due to the commission of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), the ten evil deeds, and the violation of the five precepts that one incurs this calamity.
The fourteenth is King Gaodu, who presides over the Iron Chariot Hell. The inhabitants of this hell are made of iron.

[The character 禾*并 (bìng)] is placed upon the tongue. Their bodies are scorched by chariots and glowing embers solely because they sat in empty deception, used double-tongued speech, lacked faith, treated virtuous people with contempt, and subjected others to the three blades of torture, yet claimed it was only right.
Therefore, they incur this calamity. The fifteenth is King Gongyang, who presides over the Iron Fire Hell.
Charcoal fires blaze up to the knees of the inhabitants because they abandoned the Right and entered the False, and did not believe in virtuous people or śramaṇas.

Teachers, friends, and parents provide correct instruction. Yet, many come and go treading upon and killing insects and worms. Whether they do not observe the fast, or observe the fast in mind while walking with their feet, they thereby incur this calamity.
The sixteenth is King Pingdou (Flat-Boat), who presides over the Hell of Boiling Excrement.

It is vast, long, and extremely deep; when sinners enter it, their bodies are cooked and rotted away. Worms swarm upon their persons, penetrating to the marrow and the sinews. Foul and filthy, they cannot sit still.
Seventeenth: King Yang (Yang-wang) presides over this pillar, which punishes those who practiced giving by forcing others to kill living beings to sustain themselves;
consequently, they incur this calamity. When the person’s feet reach the ground, the earth immediately blazes up.

This occurs because they were unable to endure the precepts of discipline while seated, and because they frequently walked to the houses of laypeople on their bare feet during the fast-day, thereby harming sentient beings. Eighteenth: Pingli (Ping-li).
King [Name], who presides over the Mili Hell. Within this hell are insects with mouths like iron awls that peck at people’s flesh and bones until they are completely consumed.
This is because [the king] sat idly catching and squeezing the bodily fluids of sentient beings and nourished his own body by killing living creatures; thus he incurred this calamity.
The nineteenth is King Lien-shi, who presides over the Mountain Stone Hell. Within this hell are stones as sharp as the edge of a blade, reaching as high as a person’s knee.

Some [stones] are five inches high; when one steps upon them to ascend, they may rise or fall. They sever the feet and cut the ankles; they flay the legs and snap the tendons. The stones are as sharp as knives.
On the days of the Eight Kings, one does not practice the Way; though the mind may contemplate goodness, the feet wander in dissipation, causing the six spirits to fly about.
Thus observed by the celestial palaces, this calamity is brought about. The twentieth is King Langye, who primarily presides over many [sufferings].
The Hell of Hot Winds (Liúyù). Within this hell there is a hot wind that encounters people and blows them across the ground.
It is the height of wailing and lamentation; one seeks death but cannot find it, and seeks life but cannot find it. This is caused by the torment inflicted upon others while alive.
The twenty-first is King Duguān, who presides over the Liúyù Hell. Within this hell there is a "Great Man-Eater" ghost, from whose body sixty spikes emerge.

It pierces through the person's body; fire issues from within the body and burns the person as they eat it. This is solely because of committing adultery with women and engaging with animals, and killing sentient beings;
thus one incurs this calamity. The twenty-second is King Xuanyang, who presides over the Hell of Flying Insects.
Insects fly in to devour the person without ceasing, coming from all four directions in countless numbers. This is solely because of hunting and shooting mosquitoes and gadflies.
...the retribution for this. Thus, such calamity is brought about. The twenty-third is King Taiyi (Great Unity), who presides over the River of Boiling Water Hell.

The flowing river water is hotter than boiling sesame oil in the world. It is solely because of killing living beings with nets, catching fish and gathering eggs, and drinking wine to lose the fifteen modes of conduct that one undergoes this calamity.
The twenty-fourth is King Heshi (Combined Stone), who presides over the Great...
The Grinding Hell. It is two thousand li in width and length. The hell-beings are ground like flour.

This is solely because they took pleasure in killing living beings, crushing sentient beings between stones that grind against one another, even down to insects and lice; thus they incur this calamity.

The twenty-fifth is the King of Coolness, who presides over the Cold Snow Hell. The sinners within this hell are frozen and chilled, solely because they froze living beings to death after having killed them.

They stripped others of their clothing and imprisoned sentient beings; because they failed to provide warm, harmonious garments when people were suffering from the cold, they now undergo this retribution.

The twenty-sixth [hell] is King Mūla (No-Root), who presides over the Iron Mortar Hell. He heats the mortars until they are glowing red and thrusts them into the throats of the inhabitants, so that their lips, tongues, intestines, and stomachs are all scorched and rotted away.
This is solely due to their malicious speech in seeking flavors and their evil physical conduct.
This is brought about by the mind’s contemplation of evil; therefore, one undergoes this calamity. King Zhengshi, the twenty-seventh, presided over the Iron Pillar Prison.
He would heat the pillars until they were glowing red and force people to embrace them, or lie upon beds of burning iron, where they were devoured by lust-demons.
This was solely due to the lustful thoughts, words, and deeds of their hearts and bodies; therefore, they underwent this calamity. King Gaoyuan, the twenty-eighth—
This primarily governs the Hell of Pus and Blood. [Those who] eat blood and raw flesh, give impure things to others, and are driven by greed and lust [fall here].

The twenty-ninth is King Du-jin (All-Advancing). This primarily governs the Hell of Burning Stones. The burning stones are glowing red; they cause people to sit upon them, scorching and rotting their intestines and stomachs.
[Those who fall here] all sat together without precepts, consumed the faithful offerings of others, failed to maintain the fasts and precepts, and cut off the merit of others. Thus it is said.
This is brought about by one's own actions; therefore, one undergoes this retribution. The thirtieth is King Yuandu, who presides over the Iron Wheel Hell.

A wheel of blazing red fire spontaneously appears above the heads of those who, while riding, placed their feet upon their parents, teachers, friends, kings, husbands, or those whom they especially revered;
who excessively touched the heads of others or those who are śramaṇas; and who mocked those with physical deformities, stammers, or baldness.
Treading upon the shadows of one's teachers, friends, and father, and setting fire to their heads, brings about this calamity.
This constitutes the great suffering of the *naraka* (hells) for the masses of the world. Those who commit these twenty major transgressions shall all undergo thirty minor *naraka*s in succession;

after the forms of these immeasurable kalpas of great *naraka*s have ended, they next enter the hundred and four minor *naraka*s until those kalpas are exhausted. Upon emerging from hell, they shall...
Furthermore, they shall become hungry ghosts, animals, slaves, or those of low station for billions upon billions of kalpas—equal in number to the sands of ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* oceans.
If one grain of sand represents one thousand kalpas, and this continues until all the sands of ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* oceans are exhausted, they may then again enter the human realm.

Even as a human, their mouth will be perpetually foul, their speech will be met with falsehood, they will suffer many illnesses and lack prosperity, and they will have a short lifespan. This applies to those who commit these twenty offenses. Now...

There will be no benefit in the present life; one shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the various heavens and hells. The divine spirits listen and observe, recording sins and blessings in their registers without regard for the noble or the humble.
Six times each month, they submit reports; four times each year, they conduct comprehensive reviews. On the days of these four reviews, the first day of every month is used [for this purpose].
As for the Eight Kings' Days, the Heavenly Kings compare the records of the various classes of beings among the heavenly people and examine them accordingly.

Merit is supreme. Those with blessings shall have their lifespans increased; those with transgressions shall have their lifespans diminished, and their records seized. Vast are heaven and earth, and countless are the common people.

Within all heavens and hells, there are the Great Kings of the Five Paths, the Director of Fate, the Grand Recorder, the Commandant of the Five Offices, the Messengers of the Kings of the Four Garrisons, the Great Generals who Receive Heaven’s Mandate, and others.
Throughout spring, autumn, winter, and summer, they receive Heaven’s mandate to govern and oversee, prohibiting and investigating all that is unlawful. They preside over all.
They hold the registers of the mouths of sentient beings and control the length of their lives, down to the finest division of a hair without error. The people’s voices are shrouded in darkness;
they do not understand what is recorded by the Five Officials of Heaven and Earth. They cannot know from whence they have come to life, nor where they will go when they die.
They cannot know the length of their own lifespan, nor that they are being collected and registered by the Five Officials. They do not know how to proactively perform good deeds to seek [liberation].
Peace. I did not know to perform meritorious deeds in advance to save myself from my transgressions, nor did I understand to rely upon the Triple Gem to seek salvation in future lives.

I was ignorant of seeking out and following a Daoist who observes the precepts and masters the scriptures to ask for the path that transcends the world. It is like an old, worn-out ox that is no longer fit for use;
when the master says, "This ox is old and worn out and no longer useful," it is merely a burden to its father who must labor to feed and raise it—now it brings me no benefit.
In a household, one should simply slaughter [the ox] early; thus one may obtain meat and also eliminate the afflictions. Human beings are just like this:
if they do not uphold the precepts nor perform meritorious deeds, they are like an ox that causes the household great trouble and provides no benefit to the family.

Furthermore, they are unable to sustain themselves. Human beings are born from the Way (Dao), and the vital energy of the Way nourishes them. Yet, being unwilling to revere the Way, they cannot save themselves either. They are herded by the five viscera;
upon death, they are delivered to hell, where they remain subject to the control of the King of the World. Thus it is.
The Scripture on Pure Deliverance, Scroll One
